 Jordan International Dates Festival Opens Under Royal Patronage
 10/11/2026 | 17:23:13
 Amman, Nov. 10 (Petra) -- The eighth Jordan International Dates 
Festival 2026 opened Tuesday in Amman under the patronage of His 
Majesty King Abdullah II.
 The Ministry of Agriculture organized the festival with the Khalifa 
International Award for Date Palm and Agricultural Innovation, part 
of the Zayed Humanitarian Legacy Foundation at the Presidential Court 
of the United Arab Emirates. It was held in cooperation with the 
Jordan Dates Association and the Jordan Dates Cooperative.
 Agriculture Minister Saeb Khreisat said the festival began in 2018 
and has developed institutionally through cooperation with the 
Khalifa Award, the foundation, the association, the cooperative and 
the ministry. It has become an annual gathering, he said.
 Khreisat said palm has been rooted in this part of the world for 
thousands of years, and studies confirm date palms existed in Jordan 
about 3,000 years ago.
 He added that the date industry and exports generate more than $60 
million. Investment in palm cultivation stands at about $600 million, 
and the sector has created more than 12,000 jobs, about 5,000 of them 
for women.
 Khreisat said Jordan’s Medjool dates enjoy a high global reputation 
that surpasses dates grown elsewhere. He attributed it to the Jordan 
Valley’s climate, atmospheric pressure, oxygen levels, soil and low 
elevation below sea level.
 He said the partnership between the Khalifa Award and the ministry 
extends the leadership cooperation between King Abdullah and Sheikh 
Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, president of the UAE.
 He said investments worth millions of dinars are going into 
artificial intelligence and agricultural innovation for palms and 
Medjool dates. One of the world’s largest facilities for 
localization, grading, classification and export of dates will open 
soon, he added.
 Jordan Dates Association Chairman Anwar Haddad said Medjool dates top 
the international dates market with exceptional efficiency and high 
quality. He said steady growth in the sector has doubled land prices 
in the Jordan Valley and turned previously unusable land and some 
saline water into productive palm farms. Per capita consumption is 4 
kilograms a year, he said.
 Haddad said the sector is moving toward artificial intelligence, 
modern mechanization and smart irrigation to face water scarcity and 
climate change. It is also addressing fragmented land holdings 
through collection and sorting centers.
 He said the association amended its bylaws to include all value chain 
parties, from farmers and service providers to experts and university 
professors, on a single platform.
 He said processing industries are being developed to turn production 
waste into high-value products such as biochar, date powder, date tea 
and date-based Nutella, as well as a date version of Umm Ali.
 Haddad said the eighth festival includes a specialized exhibition 
with 14 foreign countries and a scientific symposium focused on 
artificial intelligence and digitization.
 It also includes the international buyer program, which has brought 
about 80 global buyers to Amman since 2018 to conclude deals. He 
thanked the partners, led by the ministry, the Khalifa Award and the 
Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).
 Khalifa International Award for Date Palm and Agricultural Innovation 
Secretary-General Abdelouahhab Alboukhari Zaid said Jordan has 
established a distinguished position for its dates, led by Medjool, 
which has become a model of quality, economic value and 
competitiveness.
 Zaid said the next phase requires focus on three interlinked 
priorities: raising the efficiency of natural resource use, improving 
product quality and added value, and expanding marketing 
opportunities and access to international markets.
 He said the current challenge is no longer limited to increasing 
production or expanding markets. It is to sustain this success amid 
climate change, growing pressure on water resources and rising global 
quality and competitiveness requirements.
 UAE Ambassador to Jordan Sultan Al Shamsi said the festival embodies 
the depth of relations and the strategic partnership between the two 
countries. The late King Hussein bin Talal and Sheikh Zayed bin 
Sultan Al Nahyan laid the foundations, and King Abdullah and Sheikh 
Mohammed bin Zayed continue them, he said.
 Shamsi said the partnership gained new economic horizons when the 
Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement between the two 
countries entered into force in May 2025, enhancing trade and 
investment opportunities.
 He said the palm's status goes beyond its economic and nutritional 
value, as it is an integral part of Arab identity and civilizational 
heritage. 
He added that the UAE has pioneering experience in developing the 
date palm sector through scientific research, innovation and modern 
agricultural technologies. He said the UAE is keen to work with 
Jordan, exchange expertise and integrate efforts to develop the 
sector and raise quality and competitiveness.
 Shamsi said the UAE gives special importance to water security as a 
pillar of food security and sustainable development. He noted that 
the UAE, in partnership with Senegal, hosts the United Nations Water 
Conference in Abu Dhabi from Dec. 2 to 12.
 The opening ceremony honored the winners of the eighth Jordanian 
dates competition and influential figures in the sector. Several 
agreements were then signed, and the exhibition was officially opened 
with presentations by exhibiting companies.
 Regional and international organizations helped organize and support 
the festival. They include FAO, the International Center for 
Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA), the Medjool 
International Network (MIN), the Association of Agricultural Research 
Institutions in the Near East and North Africa, the Arab Organization 
for Agricultural Development, the Arab Center for the Studies of Arid 
Zones and Dry Lands (ACSAD) and the International Center for 
Biosaline Agriculture.
